alalal-e17972-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 6: whether one must always obey the higher authority.

alalal-e17972-d1e113.summary: Introduces questions on Lombard's citation of Augustine, 'consider the grades of human affairs'.

alalal-e17972-d1e125.summary: First question: whether Augustine's rule that the higher authority is to be obeyed when higher and lower command contrary things is always true.

alalal-e17972-d1e139.summary: Second question: whether the power of tyrants must be obeyed.

alalal-e17972-d1e146.summary: First objection: the Gloss on Apocalypse 2:12 says an archbishop may not lay hands on a bishop's subjects without the bishop, so an archbishop cannot command the bishop's subjects contrary to him, and the rule is not universal.

alalal-e17972-d1e174.summary: Second objection: a more immediate power has more influence; the lower power is more immediate over subjects, so in conflict the lower should prevail.

alalal-e17972-d1e192.summary: Sed contra from Boethius: whatever a lower power can do, a higher can do and more, so in conflict the lower must yield.

alalal-e17972-d1e205.summary: Solution: higher and lower authorities relate in two ways. Where the lower derives wholly from the higher, as a proconsul's from the emperor's or bishops' from the pope's, the higher remains ordinary and immediate over all subjects; Augustine speaks of this case, and there is no exception. Where both derive from a universal power that subjects the lower to the higher only in some matters, as bishop and archbishop relative to the pope, the lower can command things the higher cannot revoke.
claims: When a lower authority derives wholly from a higher one, the higher prevails in conflict.
When both derive from a common universal authority, the lower may have commands the higher cannot revoke.

alalal-e17972.summary: Article 6 asks whether Augustine's rule, that the higher authority must be obeyed when higher and lower command contrary things, always holds, and announces the question of tyrants. Objections cite the archbishop's lack of jurisdiction over a bishop's subjects and the greater immediacy of the lower power. Albert distinguishes two structures. Where the lower power derives wholly from the higher, as a proconsul's from the emperor or bishops' from the pope, the higher remains immediate over all subjects and always prevails, which is Augustine's case. Where both derive from a common universal power that subordinates them only in some matters, as with bishop and archbishop under the pope, the lower may issue commands the higher cannot revoke.
claims: When a lower authority derives wholly from a higher, the higher must be obeyed in case of conflict.
Coordinate authorities derived from a common superior may each have spheres the other cannot override.
